params.question: What distinguishes nodular episcleritis from a scleral nodule on clinical examination?

answers.text: The scleral nodule blanches with phenylephrine; the episcleral nodule does not

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The phenylephrine blanching test distinguishes episcleritis from scleritis overall, not specifically nodular from scleral nodules. Blanching indicates superficial episcleral vessel involvement.

answers.text: The episcleral nodule is freely mobile when probed with a cotton swab; the scleral nodule is fixed

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The episcleral nodule sits in the loose, vascular episcleral tissue and moves freely when swept with a cotton-tipped swab. A scleral nodule is embedded in dense scleral collagen and remains fixed.

answers.text: The episcleral nodule produces severe boring pain that wakes the patient from sleep

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Severe boring pain that wakes the patient is characteristic of scleritis, not episcleritis. Episcleral nodules cause only mild aching or irritation.

answers.text: The scleral nodule is bright red; the episcleral nodule is violaceous

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This reverses the colour pattern. Episcleritis produces bright-red superficial injection, while scleritis gives a violaceous (blue-purple) hue due to deep vessel inflammation.

overallFeedback.feedback: A freely mobile nodule confirms episcleral origin; a fixed nodule indicates scleral involvement. This distinction rests on the anatomical difference between loose episcleral tissue and dense scleral collagen.
The cotton-swab mobility test is a key bedside manoeuvre — the loose episcleral connective tissue allows nodules to shift freely, while dense scleral collagen holds scleral nodules fixed.

params.question: A 25-year-old woman with her first episode of simple episcleritis finds lubricant drops and cool compresses insufficient after five days. What is the most appropriate next step?

answers.text: Oral prednisolone 40 mg daily for two weeks

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Systemic corticosteroids are disproportionate for simple episcleritis, which is self-limiting and resolves within two to three weeks. Stepwise escalation with topical NSAIDs is the appropriate next step.
Immunosuppressive agents are reserved for scleritis with underlying systemic vasculitis. Episcleritis is benign and self-limiting; management aims at symptom relief, not immunosuppression.
Rheumatology referral is not indicated for a first episode of uncomplicated simple episcleritis. It becomes relevant for recurrent or bilateral episodes, or when scleritis is diagnosed.

Correct. The stepwise management ladder is: lubricants and cool compresses first, then topical ketorolac if symptoms persist, followed by oral flurbiprofen 100 mg TDS for more troublesome or nodular cases.

overallFeedback.feedback: The management ladder for episcleritis: lubricants and cool compresses → topical ketorolac → oral flurbiprofen 100 mg TDS. Reserve systemic immunosuppression and urgent referrals for scleritis.
Episcleritis management is conservative and stepwise — the goal is symptom relief, not cure, as the condition is self-limiting within two to three weeks.

params.question: Why must granulomatosis with polyangiitis be specifically excluded in every patient diagnosed with scleritis?

answers.text: It is the most common systemic association, present in over 50% of scleritis cases

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Rheumatoid arthritis is the most common systemic association with scleritis, present in 20–30% of cases. Granulomatosis with polyangiitis is less common but far more dangerous if missed.

answers.text: It exclusively presents with bilateral rather than unilateral scleritis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis can present with either unilateral or bilateral scleritis. Laterality does not reliably distinguish the underlying systemic cause.

answers.text: Unrecognised, it can progress to fatal renal failure through glomerulonephritis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Granulomatosis with polyangiitis is a necrotising vasculitis identified by c-ANCA. The same immune complex deposition that inflames the sclera can damage the kidneys, causing glomerulonephritis and potentially fatal renal failure.

answers.text: It is the only vasculitis that responds to topical anti-inflammatory therapy

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Scleritis involves deep scleral vasculitis that topical drugs cannot penetrate. No form of scleritis, regardless of its systemic cause, responds adequately to topical anti-inflammatory therapy alone.

overallFeedback.feedback: GPA is identified by c-ANCA and can cause fatal glomerulonephritis if missed. The bedside rule: ANCA-positive → dipstick urine → urgent nephrology referral if haematuria is found.
The bedside rule: always dipstick the urine in any c-ANCA-positive patient. Microscopic haematuria signals glomerulonephritis and demands urgent nephrology referral.

params.question: A 52-year-old man presents with deep boring eye pain that wakes him at night. Phenylephrine 2.5% produces no blanching, and his c-ANCA test returns positive. What is the most appropriate immediate action?

answers.text: Arrange same-day emergency referral to both rheumatology and nephrology

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The algorithm mandates same-day emergency referral when scleritis is associated with a positive c-ANCA. Granulomatosis with polyangiitis can cause fatal glomerulonephritis, requiring immediate rheumatology and nephrology co-management.

answers.text: Prescribe topical lubricants and review in two weeks

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Topical lubricants are appropriate for simple episcleritis. This patient has scleritis (non-blanching, boring pain) with a positive c-ANCA indicating possible granulomatosis with polyangiitis — a life-threatening condition requiring urgent specialist input.

answers.text: Start oral flurbiprofen and arrange outpatient rheumatology review within one month

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Oral flurbiprofen is second-line management for episcleritis, not scleritis. A positive c-ANCA demands urgent — not routine outpatient — referral because of the risk of active renal and pulmonary vasculitis.

answers.text: Order topical ketorolac and arrange a routine blood screen

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Topical ketorolac cannot penetrate to the deep scleral vessels involved in scleritis. A positive c-ANCA is not a routine finding — it signals necrotising vasculitis that may already be damaging the kidneys.

overallFeedback.feedback: The referral escalation ladder: simple episcleritis → primary eye care; all scleritis → rheumatology; necrotising disease or positive c-ANCA → same-day emergency rheumatology and nephrology admission.
Non-blanching redness plus positive c-ANCA is the highest-urgency combination in the algorithm — same-day emergency referral to rheumatology and nephrology is non-negotiable.
